name: Oral hygiene for scent
lead: Oral hygiene for scent refers to caring for the mouth so that breath does not detract from how a person smells to others. Roughly 85 to 90 percent of genuine bad-breath cases originate in the mouth, most commonly from bacteria on the back of the tongue.[1]
Evidence for specific interventions is weak overall; tentative support exists for tongue cleaning and antibacterial mouthwashes.[1]

paras: Poor oral hygiene allows biofilm to build up, and bacteria break down proteins into foul-smelling compounds. Gum disease, decay, dry mouth, smoking and certain foods also contribute; less commonly the source is sinus, tonsil, reflux or systemic disease.[1]

Brushing may help and flossing may be useful. There is tentative evidence for tongue cleaning and for antibacterial mouthwashes containing chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride, which can temporarily stain teeth; alcohol-containing rinses may worsen dryness. Dietary changes and chewing gum lack support.[1]
People often cannot notice their own breath, and licking the wrist is described as an unreliable test.[1] About a quarter of people seeking advice have an exaggerated concern.[1]
Reviews summarized in the sources report weak overall evidence and no strong indication of which interventions work.[1]

card.summary: Mouth care aimed at fresh breath as part of overall scent; interventions have tentative but weak evidence.

quick.overview:
Breath is part of how a person is perceived by smell, and most bad breath starts in the mouth.

Tongue cleaning and antibacterial mouthwash have tentative support, but overall evidence is weak.
quick.mechanism: Reducing bacterial biofilm on the tongue and teeth lowers production of odorous compounds.
quick.risks: Antibacterial mouthwashes can stain teeth and alcohol rinses may dry the mouth. Persistent odor can have medical causes.
